To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the AQS QBFB exhibits a capacity fade rate of 1.5% per 100 cycles and that the AQDS QBFB exhibits a lower fade rate of 0.6% per 1000 cycles.
the capacity retention rates during cycling of two QBFBs differ significantly and that the capacity fade rate in an AQDS QBFB increases with the number of cycles.

(i) the AQDS cell has better capacity retention rates than the AQS cell, (ii) the AQS cell capacity fades due to formation of hydroxide species, and (iii) the AQDS capacity fades due to bromine crossover.

the development of aqueous QBFB technology, which has the potential for high energy density and long cycle life.
the capacity retention rates during cycling of aqueous quinone-bromo flow batteries.
the development of a low cost and environmentally benign battery that is capable of storing electricity from intermittent renewable energy sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the capacity retention rates are 0.2% for the AQS cell and 0.03% for the AQDS cell, extrapolated to 5000 cycles at the same current density.
both the AQS and AQDS QBFBs exhibit promising performance and that further research and development will likely yield an aqueous QBFB capable of 5000 cycles with 100% capacity retention.
the AQS-based QBFB is not viable for long-term cycling, whereas the AQDS-based QBFB is promising but will need bromine rebalancers and/or a more effective bromine barrier to achieve long cycle life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AQDS QBFB exhibits the best capacity retention rate among the three QBFBs we have tested to date.
the capacity retention rate of the AQDS cell is limited by chemical degradation of the active species, whereas that of the AQS cell is limited by bromine crossover.
the capacity retention rates for aqueous QBFB systems can be significantly improved over previously reported results, but that the long-term cycling of such systems remains a challenge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
capacity fade rates in aqueous QBFB cycling are not negligible and that further research is needed to understand the underlying mechanisms and develop solutions.
, despite the high redox reversibility of the quinone-brome redox couples, the aqueous QBFB suffers from capacity fade due to bromine crossover and hydroxide attack on the quinone.
, while the aqueous QBFB is a promising technology, further work is needed to improve the capacity retention rate and electrolyte balance.
